weakness: The pipeline averaged the peg pose once at t=0 and then executed the whole pre-grasp/grasp sequence open-loop on that estimate; when the peg slid a few cm sideways after detection, the fingers closed on empty space or on the peg's edge and nothing checked or retried (9/10 failures).
how_found: Questioned A3 (the peg is static between detection and finger closure). A single detection followed by ~4 s of arm motion is a long open-loop window, and on a real table objects get bumped, roll or settle after being placed.
why_missed: All Phase 1 effort went into perception noise (averaging) and arm tracking error at the hole; in the default task nothing moves, so the grasp never failed and the stale-estimate window was invisible. Averaging many detections also hides motion: it gives a confident estimate of where the object was.
fix: Added wait_static (two averaged estimates 0.25 s apart must agree within 4 mm), re-measure the peg at the pre-grasp pose and re-plan if it moved more than 5 mm, and retry the whole grasp (up to 3 times) if gripper_holding() is false after the lift.
general_rule: Re-perceive the target immediately before every contact action, require it to be stationary across two estimates separated in time, and verify the result of the action (e.g. holding) with a retry loop instead of trusting an estimate taken before the arm started moving.

weakness: With a heavy (2 kg), slippery (friction 0.15) peg the single top-down grasp near the tail cannot hold it: gravity torque about the fingers makes the peg pivot until its head hits the table or jams on the rim, and the loaded arm sags and overshoots 2-3 cm at the start of every move. Grasping close to the centre of mass holds it level (v4 reached 0.8), but then the hand collides with the box face about 2 cm before the head is deep enough, which broke the default scene (base 0.2-0.7). No single grasp point satisfies both constraints.
how_found: Questioned A7 (a tail grasp holds the peg rigidly): the grasp is far from the centre of mass and the fingers rely on friction only, so mass and friction directly set whether the peg rotates in the hand. A moderate change (v3, 1 kg) did not break it, the stronger one did.
why_missed: Phase 1 chose the grasp point only from the geometric clearance needed at the end of insertion (A11), with a light, grippy object where the grasp location does not matter for holding. The two requirements on the grasp point, holding against gravity torque during transport and clearance from the target at the end of the task, were never written down together, so their conflict was invisible.
fix: Not recovered within 6 repairs (pipeline reverted to round 1). Tried: grasp 3 cm behind the centre + stepwise realignment + jam detection/back-off + pushing the tail with closed fingers when the grip slips (v4 0.8 but base 0.2-0.7 because the hand hit the box face at -2 cm); grasp 4.5 cm behind the centre to clear the face (v4 dropped to 0.1). The likely solution, not tested in budget: insert partway with the centre grasp until the hole supports the peg, release, regrasp (or push) at the tail, and finish the insertion.
general_rule: When one grasp must serve both transport and final placement, derive the grasp point from both constraints (torque from the object's centre of mass during transport, and hand clearance from the target at the end), and when they conflict plan a regrasp or hand-off part-way instead of tuning a single compromise grasp point.

weakness: The grasp point was a fixed function of the object's own geometry (a set distance behind its centre), and every move_to was planned without any scene obstacles. With an immovable block 1-2 cm beside the rear half of the peg, the open finger and the hand body came down on the block every time (10/10 failures), and nothing checked whether the hand fits there or offered an alternative.
how_found: Questioned A5/A6 (the space around the grasp point is free). The grasp was planned only from the target's pose, never from the scene; the hand is much wider (open fingers, palm) than the object it grasps, so anything within a few cm of it is a collision. A loose box at the same spot (v5) was pushed aside and did not break it, so the variation had to be immovable.
why_missed: In the default scene the only other object (the box with the hole) is far from the peg, so collision-free grasping came for free and the hand's footprint was never modelled. The pipeline even had the obstacle list available from perception but never used it.
fix: Average the obstacle boxes of all non-task objects; model the open hand as three boxes (two fingers, palm) in the grasp frame and reject grasp candidates whose hand boxes come within 1 cm of an obstacle; try tail grasp offsets in order of preference; if none is free, pick the object up wherever the hand fits, set it down 10 cm to the side away from the obstacles, release, and grasp again normally; plan transit moves with avoid=<obstacles>. Recovered in 1 repair: v6 1.0, v2 1.0, base 0.9.
general_rule: Before committing to a grasp, check the whole hand's footprint (open fingers and palm, not just the contact point) against every perceived object, search over alternative grasps when it collides, and if the task-preferred grasp is blocked, first move the object to free space with any grasp that fits and then regrasp it.

weakness: The grasp was planned purely from the object's pose, assuming the arm can comfortably reach anywhere the object might be. With the peg ~0.82 m from the robot base (inside the valid workspace, near the reach limit), the top-down pre-grasp above the tail was either unreachable (the program gave up after three identical attempts) or reached only through a long RRT detour, after which the 8 cm straight descent from that awkward configuration consumed the whole 2000-step budget.
how_found: Questioned A8: the program never considered where the robot is. The task randomises object positions over a small patch near the workspace centre, so reach margins were never exercised, while on a real table objects end up wherever the last user left them.
why_missed: In the default scenes every grasp was well inside the workspace, so move_to always succeeded quickly and reachability looked binary and free. A motion planner that reports success says nothing about how long or how well-conditioned the motion is: 'reachable' at the boundary still fails in practice.
fix: (1) If the preferred grasp point is farther than a comfortable reach (0.75 m, from the robot model; the arm's limit is ~0.85 m) from the robot base, or if its pre-grasp or grasp cannot be reached, first pick the peg at the graspable point nearest the workspace centre, carry it 15 cm inward, put it down and release; then grasp it normally. (2) Try only a few nearby grasp candidates instead of letting the planner find far-fetched detours. Recovered in 4 repairs: v9 0.9, v6 1.0, v2 1.0, base 0.9.
general_rule: Check every planned grasp against the robot's comfortable workspace (a margin inside its reach limit, not just planner success), and when the object lies outside it, first move the object toward the workspace centre with whatever grasp is easiest, then do the task grasp from there; never accept a motion the planner only finds by a long detour.

weakness: With a shelf 15 cm above the rear half of the peg, the tail grasp itself fits under it but the wrist and forearm above a top-down hand do not, so the planner (avoiding the shelf) rejected the pre-grasp; the round-3 recovery then set the peg aside 10 cm sideways, which left it under the 30 cm-wide shelf, and repeated that until the attempts ran out.
how_found: Questioned the round-3 fix itself: its hand model stopped at the palm, and the set-aside destination was chosen by distance from the obstacle's centre, never by checking that the follow-up grasp would be free there. A large, overhanging obstacle defeats both.
why_missed: The round-3 rule was implemented only for the case that broke it (a small block beside the fingers): the footprint covered what touched that block, and 'move to free space' was approximated by 'move away from the centre', which works only for small obstacles.
fix: Added the wrist/forearm column above the hand to the footprint model, and choose the put-down spot among candidate shifts (toward the workspace centre, sideways, along the object) by checking that the object fits there (including the fixture) and that the follow-up grasp is free and comfortably reachable. Recovered in 1 repair: v11 0.9, v9 0.9, v6 1.0, v2 1.0, base 0.9.
general_rule: Same as the obstacle rule of an earlier round: check the whole arm-and-hand footprint for the grasp, and when relocating an object, verify the precondition of the next action (a free, reachable grasp) at the destination before choosing it.

weakness: The grasp was computed from the peg's axis projected onto the table and placed at the height of the peg's centre, i.e. it assumed the object lies flat. With the peg leaning ~25 deg on a block, the grasp point near the low tail was 2-3 cm above the real axis and the hand was not square to it, so the fingers closed on the upper edge or missed (7/10 failures).
how_found: Questioned A1 (the peg lies flat). The code literally zeroed the vertical component of the measured axis and reused the centre's height, discarding information perception already provided; objects on a real table often lean on something. An 18 deg lean (v12) still mostly worked (0.5), so the tilt was increased.
why_missed: Every default scene places the peg flat on the table, so projecting the axis and reusing the centre height was exact; the simplification was invisible because it was never wrong in the scenes tested.
fix: Place the grasp point on the measured 3D axis (centre minus offset along the true axis, so its height follows the tilt) and orient the hand square to that axis: approach = straight down made perpendicular to the axis, closing = approach x axis. Identical to before for a flat peg; the in-hand servo already corrects the remaining tilt before insertion. Recovered in 1 repair: v13 0.9, v11 0.8, v9 0.9, v6 1.0, v2 1.0, base 0.9.
general_rule: Plan grasps from the object's full measured 6-DoF pose, never from a projection that assumes its usual resting orientation, so the grasp point lies on the object's real geometry and the hand is square to it.
